title: Introduction to Java I/O
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of introduction to java i/o and identify when it is appropriate in a Java program.
Apply at least one of the lesson topics—input and output concepts—in a small, readable example.
Identify one failure, compatibility, security, or resource-management concern and describe a safe response.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study introduction to java i/o with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you read and write local data while handling resources, paths, and malformed input safely. In this lesson, focus on input and output concepts and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Treat console input as untrusted text. Validate format and range before using it, account for token-versus-line reading, and give users a clear way to correct invalid input. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

content_blocks.title: How the pieces fit
content_blocks.text: Connect input and output concepts with streams as data flows before choosing an implementation. The example is a small, observable case; extend it by changing one input and checking a boundary, invalid value, or compatibility limit where relevant.

items.title: Input and output concepts
items.text: Treat console input as untrusted text. Validate format and range before using it, account for token-versus-line reading, and give users a clear way to correct invalid input.

items.title: Streams as data flows
items.text: A stream pipeline describes transformations over a source. Intermediate operations are lazy; a terminal operation triggers work, and stream instances should not be reused after a terminal operation.

items.title: Byte-oriented versus character-oriented APIs
items.text: Primitive variables store values of the eight primitive types. Choose a type that represents the domain and range required; use exact decimal arithmetic for monetary values when appropriate.

items.title: Blocking I/O basics
items.text: Concurrency introduces shared-state ordering and cancellation concerns. Prefer task abstractions and immutable data where possible, coordinate access explicitly, and always define shutdown, timeout, and failure behavior.

content_blocks.run_instructions: Choose byte streams for binary data and character-oriented APIs for text. For ordinary Java SE examples, use JDK 25, save a complete class as Main.java, and run `javac Main.java` followed by `java Main`. CodeLeaf does not execute Java in the browser; use a local JDK for these examples. Preview-only and configuration-file examples have their own version or filename notes.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original example, remove any temporary output files it created, and rerun the baseline case. Do not leave credentials, generated private data, or large test files in the project directory.

content_blocks.title: Professional habit
content_blocks.text: Keep one clear hypothesis per experiment. Check the version, read the error message, test boundaries, and record what evidence supports your conclusion.
